name: DS1307ZN+T&R
title: DS1307 I²C real-time clock with 56 bytes of battery-backed RAM
summary: The DS1307 keeps seconds, minutes, hours, day of week, date, month and year in BCD registers, with leap years handled through 2100 and a choice of 12-hour or 24-hour time. It also holds 56 bytes of general-purpose RAM. A host reaches both over a standard-mode (100 kHz) I²C bus. It runs from a 32.768 kHz crystal, senses loss of its 5 V supply, and switches to a backup cell, on which the clock keeps running at about 300 nA.
key_figures: 300 nA typ, 500 nA max, oscillator on, SQW/OUT off

notes: A + in the part number marks a lead-free, RoHS-compliant package.
On the top mark, a + means lead-free and an N means the industrial temperature grade.

pins.name: X1
pins.function: Oscillator input, one end of the 32.768 kHz crystal. The oscillator expects a crystal specified for a 12.5 pF load. An external 32.768 kHz oscillator may drive X1 instead.

pins.name: X2
pins.function: Oscillator output, the other end of the crystal. It floats when X1 is driven by an external oscillator.

pins.name: VBAT
pins.function: Backup supply from a 3 V lithium cell or another source, kept within 2.0 V to 3.5 V. Series diodes between the cell and this pin can stop the part working properly. Ground it when no backup is fitted. Access to the clock and RAM stops below the power-fail level, nominally 1.25 × VBAT. A lithium cell of 48 mAh or more keeps the part running for over 10 years without main power at +25 °C. UL recognized against reverse charging current into a lithium cell.

pins.name: SDA
pins.function: I²C data in and out. Open drain; needs a pullup resistor, which may go to up to 5.5 V whatever VCC is.

pins.name: SCL
pins.function: I²C clock in, which times every bit on the bus. Its pullup may go to up to 5.5 V whatever VCC is.

pins.name: SQW/OUT
pins.function: With SQWE set, a square wave at 1 Hz, 4.096 kHz, 8.192 kHz or 32.768 kHz; otherwise the level of the OUT bit. Open drain; needs a pullup of up to 5.5 V whatever VCC is. Works from either VCC or VBAT. May be left open when unused.

pins.name: VCC
pins.function: Main supply. Within its normal range the part can be read and written. With a backup fitted and VCC under the trip level, reads and writes are blocked while timekeeping goes on.

circuits.title: Typical operating circuit
circuits.description: A host processor talks to the DS1307 over SCL and SDA, each held up to VCC by its own pullup RPU, sized from the bus rise time and bus capacitance. A 32.768 kHz crystal sits across X1 and X2 with no other parts. A third pullup to VCC serves the open-drain SQW/OUT pin, which leaves the circuit as an output. A cell from VBAT to ground keeps the clock running when VCC is gone.

where.RPU: pullup resistor on SCL and on SDA
where.tr: rise time of SDA and SCL, 1000 ns max
where.Cb: load on a single bus line, 400 pF max

equations.name: Power-fail trip voltage
equations.expr: VPF = 1.25 × VBAT (1.216 × VBAT min, 1.284 × VBAT max)

where.VPF: VCC level under which the part ignores its inputs and ends any access
where.VBAT: backup cell voltage, specified at 3.0 V

operation.text: As VCC falls under 1.25 × VBAT, an access under way is cut off, the address counter resets and inputs are ignored, so a failing system cannot write bad data. Once VCC drops below VBAT the part moves to its low-current backup mode. Rising again, it returns to VCC when VCC exceeds VBAT + 0.2 V, and answers inputs again above 1.25 × VBAT.
A 32.768 kHz crystal across X1 and X2 needs no resistors or capacitors outside. With a crystal to Table 1, start-up usually takes under one second.

Accuracy depends on the crystal's own tolerance and on how closely the oscillator's load matches the load the crystal was cut for. Temperature drift of the crystal adds error, and noise coupled into the oscillator can make the clock gain time.

Put a local ground plane on layer 2 under the crystal and the X1, X2 pins. Keep signal traces out of the package's upper-left quarter, next to the crystal pins, unless ground plane separates the trace from the part.
Addresses 00h to 07h hold the clock registers and 08h to 3Fh the 56 RAM bytes. In a multibyte transfer the pointer wraps from 3Fh back to 00h.

Every time and date register holds BCD. The day-of-week counter steps at midnight; what its values mean is up to the user so long as they run in sequence. Invalid time or date values give undefined behaviour. Bit 7 of register 00h, CH, stops the oscillator when 1 and runs it when 0; stopping it lowers the backup current to IBATDR. At first power-up the registers typically read 01/01/00 01 00:00:00 (MM/DD/YY DOW HH:MM:SS) with CH set to 1.

Bit 6 of the hours register picks the mode, 1 for 12-hour. In 12-hour mode bit 5 reads 1 for PM; in 24-hour mode bit 5 serves as a further tens-of-hours bit, for hours 20 to 23. Write the hours again after changing the mode.

Reads and writes of time and date go through a set of user buffers. Every I²C START copies the running registers into them, so a read stays consistent while the clock ticks. Writing the seconds register resets the divider chain; a write takes effect on the DS1307's acknowledge. After that reset the other time and date registers have to be written within one second to avoid a rollover.

OUT (bit 7) sets the level on SQW/OUT while the square wave is off: 1 gives high, 0 gives low. SQWE (bit 4) turns the square wave on, at a rate set by RS1 and RS0. At 1 Hz the clock registers change on the square wave's falling edge. At first power-up OUT and SQWE are typically 0 and RS1, RS0 typically 1.

The DS1307 is a slave only, in standard mode (100 kHz); a master drives SCL and makes every START and STOP. A transfer can begin only on an idle bus, with both lines high. SDA may change only while SCL is low; SDA falling with SCL high is a START, SDA rising with SCL high is a STOP. Bytes go most significant bit first, each followed by an acknowledge clock in which the receiver pulls SDA low. A master reading data ends by not acknowledging the last byte, so the slave lets SDA go and the master can send STOP.

After START the master sends 1101000 plus a 0 for write. The DS1307 acknowledges, takes the next byte as the register pointer, then accepts any number of data bytes, acknowledging each one; the pointer steps after every byte. STOP ends the write.

After START the master sends 1101000 plus a 1 for read. The DS1307 acknowledges and sends bytes from the current pointer, which steps after each byte. Without a pointer write first, reading starts at the last stored pointer. The master ends with a not-acknowledge, then STOP. To read from a chosen address, write the pointer, then send a repeated START with the read address.
